profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a university-affiliated sustainability innovation lab that is preparing a two-page concept note for a European funding call on interdisciplinary methods for studying innovation pathways. The seed idea is a project titled 'Constellation Analysis as a Means of Interdisciplinary Innovation Research – Theory Formation from the Bottom Up,' and the team wants to position the method as both theoretically generative and useful across technology, sustainability, and governance contexts. The agenda is to generate 3-4 candidate project framings, decide what kinds of empirical materials could anchor the method section, and sketch what a small pilot and validation component might look like in the concept note. The expected outcome is a shortlist of promising concept directions and a shared sense that one of them can be written up immediately after the meeting, even though some operational details remain unspoken.

members.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
members.expertise: Qualitative methodology, science and technology studies, comparative case reconstruction, grounded theory-inspired analysis
members.background: Lena is a senior researcher who has led method-heavy work packages in sustainability and socio-technical transition projects. She is known for translating abstract methodological traditions into fundable research designs without making them look merely instrumental.
members.private_state: She wants the concept note to protect the methodological core of Constellation Analysis and to leave room for publishable theory-building rather than letting the project become mainly a facilitation service for partners.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bottom-up' design means starting from richly reconstructed empirical material and allowing conceptual categories to emerge inductively before any practical framing is imposed.

An 'innovation biography' is a historically extended trajectory of one innovation process, often covering multiple phases, actor constellations, infrastructures, and regulatory shifts over several years.
A 'convincing pilot' for a method proposal mainly has to demonstrate analytic tractability and conceptual yield, even if it uses retrospective or archived materials rather than a live field setting.

When people say 'strategic experimentation' in a methodological context, they usually mean varying the analytical configuration or model interpretation to see how alternative constellation framings change the explanation of the same case.
Nonhuman elements such as standards, devices, platforms, funding rules, and infrastructures are automatically part of the constellation even if no one names them explicitly.

members.name: Jonas Meier
members.role: Partnerships and Impact Lead, Sustainability Innovation Hub
members.expertise: Transdisciplinary project design, public-sector innovation partnerships, stakeholder process design, funder-facing framing
members.background: Jonas previously worked in municipal innovation programs and now helps research teams package complex ideas into proposals that read as concrete, collaborative, and useful to external partners. He often serves as the bridge between academic teams and implementation-oriented funders.
members.private_state: He wants the concept note to feel immediately legible to reviewers and partner organizations, and he worries that a heavily methodological framing will sound detached unless the project visibly starts from real problems and produces something partners can use quickly.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bottom-up' design means beginning from field-defined challenges and letting stakeholders surface the relevant actors and influences from their own practical standpoint.

An 'innovation biography' is a compact narrative of a concrete initiative or solution journey that can be assembled in a manageable way through a few interviews, workshop outputs, and project documents.
A 'convincing pilot' should prove that the method works in an ongoing collaboration and produces a visible output that partners recognize as useful within the project timeframe.

When people say 'strategic experimentation,' they usually mean trying different strategic options in practice—such as governance moves, coordination formats, or policy actions—and using the constellation map to inform those choices.
If a project is described as partner-relevant, the key factors in the constellation will mostly be those current participants can name and act on directly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the project should be 'bottom-up.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means inductive theory formation from detailed empirical reconstruction toward emergent conceptual patterns, with categories arising from analysis rather than being predefined.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means starting from stakeholder-experienced sustainability problems and building the inquiry outward from what field actors identify as relevant.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are positively associated with openness and non-imposition, so the phrase creates an immediate sense of alignment; in an early brainstorming meeting, neither expects that 'bottom-up' itself needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'convincing pilot' has to prove
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the concept note needs a 'convincing pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the pilot is convincing if it shows the method can reconstruct a constellation rigorously and generate analytically interesting patterns from one well-documented retrospective case.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the pilot is convincing if it shows a partner can use the method in a live setting and get an output that is obviously useful, such as a decision-relevant map or workshop result.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the surface, both are just talking about demonstrating that the method 'works'; because the meeting is for idea generation rather than planning execution, they do not naturally compare their implicit standards of proof.

misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes each biography covers the long arc of an innovation process, including emergence, setbacks, adaptation, diffusion, and institutional embedding, along with human and nonhuman elements such as infrastructures, standards, and policy regimes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes each biography is a bounded, partner-legible account of a specific initiative, centered on organizations, decision episodes, and practical obstacles that current stakeholders can recount without a large historical reconstruction effort.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term sounds specialized and shared, so it functions as a false marker of common methodology; the scope difference mainly affects later workload and evidence expectations, not the immediate surface coherence of the discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What is being 'experimented' on in strategic experimentation
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention 'strategic experimentation' as a validation component.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines experimenting on the analytical representation itself—for example, testing how different ways of grouping factors, drawing boundaries, or modeling relations change the interpretation of the same case and the robustness of the emerging theory.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines experimenting on the partners' strategic options—for example, using the constellation map to compare different intervention choices such as sequencing stakeholders differently, changing governance arrangements, or trying an alternative implementation step in practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'strategic experimentation' sounds sufficiently technical to imply shared understanding, and both associate it with validation through trying alternatives; the unnoticed gap is not whether to experiment, but whether the manipulated object is the analytic model or the real-world strategy.

turns.inner_thought: If this note is going to be worth writing, it has to protect the methodological core. 'Bottom-up' needs to signal genuine inductive theory formation from reconstructed empirical material, not generic responsiveness to partner agendas. I need to make theory-building the anchor, but in a way that still sounds fundable.
turns.utterance: Maybe the cleanest way in is to position Constellation Analysis as a genuinely bottom-up route to theory formation in complex innovation processes. If we get that sentence right, the rest of the note can hang together quite naturally.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's exactly the right flag. If we say bottom-up, reviewers and partners will hear that we begin from sustainability challenges people already recognize and build outward from there. That makes the proposal legible and avoids the impression that we're imposing a method for its own sake.
turns.utterance: Yes, and it will land even better if that bottom-up angle feels grounded in sustainability challenges people already recognize. Then it reads as open and useful rather than method-first in a narrow way.

turns.inner_thought: A comparative design gives me room for analytic ambition. If we compare several innovation biographies, we can reconstruct long trajectories and identify recurring constellation patterns across sectors. That keeps this from shrinking into a single service-oriented case and opens a path to publishable conceptual work.
turns.utterance: One framing that could work well is a comparative one: say, three innovation biographies across quite different domains, and then use that comparison to identify recurring constellation patterns. That gives us both empirical grip and a clear route to theory formation.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if the biographies are compact and partner-legible, this becomes easy to sell. We should choose initiatives that are concrete, recognizable, and narratable without a huge reconstruction effort: municipal heat planning, a food-sharing platform, a repair network. Different enough to show transferability, manageable enough to sound real.
turns.utterance: I can already see how to make that concrete. We could pick something like municipal heat planning, a food-sharing platform, and a repair-network initiative—different enough to show breadth, but still easy to communicate as a set.

turns.inner_thought: We also need the pilot to prove analytic tractability and conceptual yield. Ideally it should be a richly documented case where the constellation can be reconstructed rigorously from accessible material. I don't need a live setting; I need something that demonstrates the method works as an analytic instrument.
turns.utterance: And whatever framing we choose, the concept note will need a convincing pilot. I think we should describe one case that gives us rich, accessible material so we can show the method's value very clearly.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—a convincing pilot has to show that someone can actually use the approach and get a visible output within the project. If I phrase it in terms of rich, accessible material and clear value, that still leaves room for the partner-facing case I want.
turns.utterance: I agree. If we can point to a convincing pilot where the material is strong and the value comes through quickly, that will do a lot of work for the note.

turns.inner_thought: I should quietly define what these biographies require without making it sound burdensome. For me they must include interviews, documents, policy shifts, standards, infrastructures, and turning points over time—otherwise the constellations become too actor-centered and thin.
turns.utterance: For the method section, I'd make clear that each innovation biography is built from multiple kinds of material before we compare across cases. That helps the biographies feel genuinely substantive rather than just illustrative vignettes.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine, and I can translate it into something practical. In my head the biographies can be assembled efficiently through workshops, a few interviews, and project materials centered on key actors, bottlenecks, and memorable decision points. That also keeps the bottom-up logic visibly tied to what stakeholders themselves surface.
turns.utterance: Yes, and we can make that sound manageable by showing how the innovation biographies can be assembled in a structured way with partners. That keeps the bottom-up logic visible and reassures reviewers that the design is doable.

turns.inner_thought: We also need a validation component that remains methodological. Strategic experimentation can do that if we vary the constellation configuration analytically—groupings, boundaries, relations—and see whether the explanatory pattern holds across alternative framings of the same case.
turns.utterance: I think we should also add strategic experimentation toward the end as a validation component. Framed carefully, that lets us test different configurations and see what yields the most robust results.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Strategic experimentation will sound strong if it suggests trying different strategic options in practice and comparing what the map makes visible for decision-making. 'Different configurations' and 'robust results' are exactly the kind of language that can carry both credibility and usefulness.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's a strong phrase for the note. It makes the design sound active rather than descriptive, and it gives us a neat way to talk about learning from different configurations.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If I summarize now, I can stabilize the structure without reopening definitions. Bottom-up reconstruction, pattern finding across biographies, a convincing pilot, then validation through strategic experimentation—that is enough of a scaffold for me to write the methodological backbone the way I need it.
turns.utterance: So the overall arc would be: bottom-up reconstruction, pattern finding across the innovation biographies, a convincing pilot, and then validation through strategic experimentation. On two pages, that's actually quite a coherent story.

turns.inner_thought: Great—I'll turn that into something partner-facing and legible. In my draft, bottom-up biographies will read as problem-grounded, the convincing pilot will signal visible usefulness, and strategic experimentation will suggest actionable learning. Lena can then add the methodological depth underneath.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll draft a partner-facing version around bottom-up innovation biographies, a convincing pilot, and strategic experimentation, and you can build out the methodological backbone. That should give us a solid first concept note by later today.
